Epidermis.description: The epidermis is the thin, outer layer of skin, made of keratinised stratified squamous epithelium. Its cells are made in the basal layer, move upward, flatten and fill with keratin until they die and shed from the surface. Melanocytes sit among the basal cells and pass the pigment melanin to neighbouring keratinocytes.
clinical: Psoriasis
A chronic inflammatory disease in which keratinocytes turn over far faster than normal, so the epidermis thickens and silvery scales form.
Bullous pemphigoid
An autoimmune blistering disease in which antibodies attack hemidesmosome proteins in the basal layer, so the epidermis separates from the dermis and tense blisters form.
Keloid
Excess collagen deposited after injury grows beyond the original wound edges, unlike a hypertrophic scar, which stays within them.
Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)
An autoimmune disease in which excess collagen builds up in the dermis, making the skin thick and hard, and it can also affect internal organs.
Lipoma
A benign, usually painless tumour of mature fat cells that forms a soft, mobile lump in the subcutaneous fat.
Erythema nodosum
Tender red nodules, usually on the shins, caused by inflammation of the fibrous septa that divide the subcutaneous fat.

Hair follicle.description: A hair follicle is a tube of epidermis that grows down into the dermis and makes the hair. Matrix cells in the bulb at its base divide rapidly to form the hair shaft and inner root sheath. The dermal papilla, a small cluster of dermal cells tucked into the base of the bulb, regulates hair growth and the hair cycle.
clinical: Alopecia areata
An autoimmune condition in which immune cells attack growing (anagen) hair follicles, causing patchy hair loss.
Hidradenitis suppurativa
A chronic, painful inflammatory disease of hair follicles in the armpits and groin, where blocked follicles rupture into abscesses and sinus tracts.

Glands.description: Armpit skin has several kinds of gland. Eccrine sweat glands open onto the skin surface and cool the body by evaporation, apocrine glands open into hair follicles and make a thick, protein-rich secretion that becomes odorous when skin bacteria break it down, and sebaceous glands release oily sebum to lubricate hair and skin. The arrector pili muscles attached to hair follicles pull the hairs upright.
clinical: Acne vulgaris
Acne forms when hair follicles and their attached sebaceous glands become blocked with excess sebum and skin bacteria, producing blackheads and inflamed spots.
Primary focal hyperhidrosis
Excessive sweating from overactive eccrine glands with no underlying cause, most often affecting the armpits, palms and soles.

Vessels & nerves.description: Blood reaches the skin through arterioles in a deep plexus at the junction of dermis and hypodermis and a subpapillary plexus in the upper dermis, with capillary loops rising into each dermal papilla to feed the avascular epidermis. Cutaneous nerves run through the deep dermis and hypodermis and branch to free nerve endings that sense pain and temperature. Hair follicle nerve endings wrap around each follicle and detect hair movement.
clinical: Herpes zoster (shingles)
Reactivation of the chickenpox virus in a sensory ganglion causes a painful, blistering rash along the skin area supplied by one cutaneous nerve (a dermatome).
Infantile haemangioma
A benign tumour of blood vessel-lining cells that appears in the first weeks of life, grows over the first months and then slowly shrinks, usually disappearing over the following years.
Loss of vibration sense
Vibration sense depends on large myelinated fibres, including those from Pacinian corpuscles, and is one of the first senses lost in peripheral neuropathy such as diabetic neuropathy.
Leprosy
Mycobacterium leprae damages peripheral nerves, causing loss of sensation in numb, pale or reddish patches of skin.

parts.description: Melanocytes are neural-crest-derived dendritic cells that sit singly in the basal layer, at roughly one for every ten basal keratinocytes. Their long dendrites run up between the spinous cells and hand melanosomes (melanin-filled organelles) to about 36 keratinocytes each, forming the epidermal melanin unit; the melanin caps each keratinocyte nucleus to shield its DNA from ultraviolet light. In H&E sections they look like pale, clear cells with dark nuclei among the basal cells, and melanoma arises from them.

Hypodermis septa are the fibrous connective-tissue partitions (retinacula cutis) that run down from the dermis and divide the subcutaneous fat into lobules. They anchor the skin to the deep fascia and carry the larger blood vessels and nerves that supply it. In a section they appear as bands of dense collagen with fibroblasts between the fat lobules, and inflammation of them produces erythema nodosum, a tender red nodule typically on the shins.

Adipocytes are the large, unilocular fat cells that make up the hypodermal lobules. Each cell holds a single large lipid droplet that pushes its flattened nucleus and thin rim of cytoplasm against the cell membrane; in H&E sections, where the lipid is dissolved during processing, the cells look clear, with a crescent of nucleus pressed against the edge (a signet-ring appearance). The lobules are separated by fibrous septa and supplied by small arterioles and capillaries, and the cells store energy as triglyceride.

The hair bulb (matrix) is the expanded, onion-shaped base of a growing (anagen) hair follicle, cupped over the dermal papilla. Its matrix keratinocytes are among the fastest-dividing cells in the body, and their daughter cells move upward to form the hair shaft and the inner root sheath. Melanocytes in the bulb pass melanin to the developing cortex, so chemotherapy that halts these divisions causes the hair loss called anagen effluvium.

The eccrine duct basal layer is the outer layer of small cuboidal epithelial cells that surrounds the inner luminal cells of the eccrine sweat duct and rests on its basement membrane. Together the two layers form the duct wall, which reabsorbs sodium and chloride from the secreted sweat as it passes to the surface. In a section it appears as the outer ring of cells around the duct lumen, nearest the surrounding dermis.

The eccrine basement membrane is the thin basal lamina that wraps the secretory coil and separates its cells from the surrounding dermal connective tissue. It gives the coil mechanical support and anchors its secretory and myoepithelial cells, and it is made of type IV collagen and laminin. In a section stained with PAS (periodic acid-Schiff), it shows as a fine magenta outline around each tubule.

Apocrine sweat gland: a large coil of wide-lumened secretory tubules in the deep dermis and hypodermis of the axilla, areola and anogenital skin. Its cuboidal to columnar cells show apical blebs (snouts) and release a viscous, protein- and lipid-rich secretion that is odourless until skin bacteria break it down. Active from puberty and under sympathetic adrenergic control.

The apocrine duct is the short, narrow passage that carries secretion from the apocrine coil towards the skin, lined by a double layer of cuboidal cells. It opens into the upper hair follicle (infundibulum) above the entry of the sebaceous duct, so the secretion reaches the surface only by travelling up the follicle. In a section, its two cell layers and small lumen distinguish it from the larger secretory coil.

The apocrine duct basal layer is the outer of the two cell layers that form the wall of the apocrine duct, resting on the basement membrane. Its small cuboidal cells surround the inner luminal layer, which lines the lumen and carries secretion up towards the follicle. In a section, the two layers of the apocrine duct are told apart by the outer basal cells lying against the dermal connective tissue.

The apocrine basement membrane is the thin basal lamina that surrounds each apocrine secretory tubule, separating its secretory and myoepithelial cells from the dermal connective tissue of the axilla. It supports the wide-lumened coil and holds its cells in place, and it is made of type IV collagen and laminin. Its periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining makes it easy to trace around the wide tubules in an apocrine section.

Cutaneous arterioles are small, muscular-walled branches of the deep cutaneous plexus, which lies at the junction of the dermis and hypodermis and also supplies the fat lobules, follicles and glands. From there they rise through the reticular dermis to the subpapillary plexus, and their smooth-muscle walls control how much blood enters the skin. Arteriovenous anastomoses, direct arteriole-to-venule shunts (abundant as glomus bodies in the fingertips), can bypass the capillaries to regulate heat loss.

Cutaneous venules collect blood from the capillary loops and drain it into the subpapillary and deep venous plexuses, which run alongside the arterial plexuses. The smallest postcapillary venules are the sites where leukocytes leave the bloodstream during inflammation, and in a section inflamed venules are often ringed by cuffs of white cells. They have thinner walls and wider lumens than arterioles.

The subpapillary plexus is a horizontal network of arterioles and venules at the junction of the papillary and reticular dermis. Short branches from it rise to form the capillary loop in each dermal papilla, and its venous part holds a large share of the blood in the skin, making it an important blood reservoir. Its venous blood contributes to heat loss and to the pink colour of the skin.

Papillary capillary loops are the hairpin-shaped capillaries that rise into each dermal papilla and return to the subpapillary plexus. They supply the avascular epidermis by diffusion, and their dilation causes flushing; pressing on red skin briefly blanches it, which helps distinguish erythema from purpura. In a section, each loop appears as a small capillary with red blood cells in its lumen, sitting within a papilla.

Free nerve endings are the naked terminal branches of thin sensory axons (myelinated Aδ and unmyelinated C fibres) that lose their Schwann cell sheath and end between the epidermal keratinocytes or in the dermis. They are the most widespread cutaneous receptors, signalling pain, temperature and itch. Their cell bodies lie in dorsal root ganglia, and because the fine endings are hard to see, they are best demonstrated with nerve-specific immunostains such as PGP 9.5.

The Pacinian axon terminal is the unmyelinated end of a large, myelinated Aβ sensory axon that runs into a Pacinian corpuscle. The axon loses its myelin as it enters the corpuscle and runs along the centre of the corpuscle as a single naked terminal, where its membrane converts deformation of the lamellae into nerve impulses. In a section it appears as the central core of the corpuscle, surrounded by the concentric lamellae.
